hangeul.title: Hangeul
hangeul.desc: Learn all 40 characters, stroke order and pronunciation.

section.tocDesc: Explore the Korean writing system step by step.
section.introP1: Hangeul is the Korean writing system, created in 1443 by King Sejong the Great and a team of scholars. Before Hangeul, Koreans used Classical Chinese characters (Hanja), which took years to master and were accessible only to the elite.
section.introP2: King Sejong believed that every person — regardless of their social class — deserved to be able to read and write. He designed Hangeul to be intuitive and easy to learn. Legend says "a wise man can learn it in a morning, a fool can learn it in ten days."
section.introP3: The system was published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum ("The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People"). Today, Hangeul is celebrated every year on October 9th (Hangeul Day) and is widely regarded as one of the most logical and scientifically designed writing systems in the world.
section.jamoP1: The genius of Hangeul lies in how its characters (called jamo) were designed. Each consonant shape represents the position of the mouth, tongue, or throat when making the sound.
section.jamoConsonantP1: The basic consonant shapes are pictographic — they depict the speech organs in the act of producing the sound:
section.jamoConsonantList: ㄱ (g): shape of the tongue touching the soft palate | ㄴ (n): shape of the tongue tip touching the alveolar ridge | ㅁ (m): shape of the lips closed | ㅅ (s): shape of a tooth | ㅇ (ng): shape of the throat (circle)
section.jamoCosmologyP1: Vowels are built from just three fundamental strokes, each representing one of the three elements of Eastern cosmology:
section.jamoCosmologyHeaven: Heaven — the round dot (·), representing the sky above
section.jamoCosmologyEarth: Earth — the horizontal stroke (ㅡ), representing the flat ground
section.jamoCosmologyHuman: Human — the vertical stroke (ㅣ), representing a person standing upright
section.jamoVowelBuildP1: All vowels are combinations of these three elements. For example: ㅏ (a) = vertical stroke + dot to the right (person facing the sun). ㅓ (eo) = dot to the left + vertical stroke (person facing away from the sun).
section.consonantsIntro: Korean has 19 consonants: 14 basic and 5 double (tense). Each basic consonant shape represents the position of your mouth when you make the sound.
section.doubleConsonantsIntro: Double consonants are made by writing the basic form twice. They are pronounced with tighter throat muscles and no aspiration — a sharp, tense sound.
section.vowelsIntro: Korean has 21 vowels: 10 basic and 11 compound. They are all built from the three cosmological elements (·, ㅡ, ㅣ).
section.compoundVowelsIntro: Compound vowels combine two basic vowels into one. For example: ㅘ (wa) = ㅗ (o) + ㅏ (a).
section.silentIeungRule: Vowels never stand alone in Korean. When a syllable starts with a vowel sound, you must add the silent consonant ㅇ (ieung) as a placeholder. For example, the sound "a" is written 아 (ㅇ + ㅏ), not just ㅏ by itself.
section.syllablesIntro: Korean characters are grouped into syllable blocks. Each block represents one syllable and contains 2 to 3 characters arranged in a square:
section.syllablesBlockExplanation: The position of the vowel determines the layout: vertical vowels (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ) go to the right of the initial consonant, horizontal vowels (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ) go below it.

level1.desc: Master the basics — greetings, essentials and everyday words.

intro.description: Start your Korean journey with the most essential words and phrases. By the end of this level, you'll be able to handle basic social situations with confidence.
intro.obj2: Say thank you, sorry and excuse me
intro.officialInfo: TOPIK I (Level 1-2) is the beginner tier of the official Korean proficiency exam, recognized by the Korean government and universities worldwide. Level 1 demonstrates basic conversational ability for everyday tasks (introducing yourself, ordering food, asking simple questions). It's commonly required for Korean language study visas (D-4), and higher TOPIK scores (3+) are needed for university admission (D-2 visa) and many work visas (E-series).

c.intro: In this first lesson you'll learn the essential Korean greetings and expressions you need to navigate any social situation. Korean has different levels of formality — we focus on the formal polite form (합니다체, hamnida-che), which is the safest choice with strangers, elders, and at work.
c.ex1: Hello! (formal, used any time of day)
c.greetingExplain: 안녕하세요 is the universal Korean greeting. It works for "hello", "good morning", "good afternoon", and even "how are you?". It literally means "Are you at peace?" and is used with anyone you need to be polite with.
c.tipInformalHello: With close friends your age, you can use the short form 안녕 (annyeong). But always default to 안녕하세요 if you're unsure — it's never wrong to be too polite in Korean!
c.practiceRepeatQ1: How do you greet your teacher?
c.practiceRepeatQ2: How do you greet a friend informally?
c.introBreakdown: This is the most basic sentence pattern in Korean. 저 (jeo) is the humble form of "I" — use it in formal situations. 는 (neun) marks the topic of the sentence. 입니다 (imnida) is the formal copula, equivalent to "am" or "is". Simply replace [name] with your name or a noun (job title, nationality…).
c.exEmma: I am Emma. I am an engineer.
c.meetExplain: 만나서 반갑습니다 is used when meeting someone for the first time. 만나서 means "having met" and 반갑습니다 means "I am glad/happy". Together: "I am glad to have met you."
c.dlgMeet3: I am Minsu. Nice to meet you.
c.dlgMeet4: I am Emma. Nice to meet you!
c.cultureBowText: When meeting someone for the first time, Koreans bow slightly (about 15°) while saying 만나서 반갑습니다. The deeper the bow, the more respect you show. In business settings, you may also exchange business cards with both hands while bowing.
c.thankSorryExplain: These two expressions are among the most important in Korean. 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is the formal way to say thank you. 죄송합니다 (joesonghamnida) is the formal way to apologize. Both end in 합니다, the formal polite ending.
c.tipFormalityLevels: Korean has three levels of "thank you": 감사합니다 (very formal — strangers, work, elders) → 고마워요 (polite casual — acquaintances) → 고마워 (informal — close friends). Similarly for sorry: 죄송합니다 (formal) → 미안해요 (polite casual) → 미안 (informal).
c.practiceThankSorry: What would you say in these situations?
c.practiceTS_Q1: Someone holds the door for you
c.practiceTS_Q3: Your friend gives you a gift
c.byeExplain: Korean has two different goodbyes depending on who is leaving. If the other person is leaving and you're staying, say 안녕히 가세요 (go in peace). If you're the one leaving and the other person stays, say 안녕히 계세요 (stay in peace). If both people are leaving, both say 안녕히 가세요.
c.dlgBye1: I will be going now. Thank you!
c.dlgBye2: Goodbye! (to someone leaving — go in peace)
c.dlgBye3: Goodbye! (to someone staying — stay in peace)
c.cultureByeText: In Korean culture, the person of lower status (younger, student, employee) usually says goodbye first. It's also common to bow slightly when saying goodbye, especially in formal situations. When in doubt, wait for the other person to initiate the farewell.
c.tipNe: 네 (ne) doesn't just mean "yes" — Koreans use it constantly as a listening signal, like "uh-huh" or "I see" in English. You'll hear it in conversations to show that the listener is paying attention. Don't be surprised if someone says 네 several times while you're speaking!

ex.e1q: How do you say "Hello" in formal Korean?
ex.m5q: You're leaving a shop. The shopkeeper stays. What do you say?

c.intro: Numbers appear everywhere — in prices, dates, phone numbers, times. In this lesson you'll master the Sino-Korean number system, the most widely used in daily life.
c.tipTwoSystems: Korean has TWO number systems that coexist: Sino-Korean (borrowed from Chinese, used for money, dates, minutes, phone numbers) and Native Korean (used for counting objects, age, hours). We start with Sino-Korean because it's used more often and is simpler.
c.tipYuk: Pay attention to 육 (yuk, six) — when it follows a vowel, you may hear it pronounced as 륙 (ryuk) due to sound changes. For now, just focus on 육.
c.ctaMidSub: Lock in what you've learned with some easy exercises before moving on.
c.ruleBigExplain: To build numbers above 10, simply combine the digits. 20 is literally "two tens" (이십). 35 is "three tens five" (삼십오). No irregular forms — it's all perfectly logical!
c.phoneExplain: Koreans read phone numbers digit by digit, pronouncing each number individually. 0 is read as 공 (gong) instead of 영 (yeong) in phone contexts. The dashes or spaces separate logical groups.
c.culturePhoneText: All Korean mobile numbers start with 010 (previously 011, 016, etc.). Korean landlines start with a 2 or 3 digit area code. Sharing phone numbers is very common when meeting new colleagues, and KakaoTalk (카카오톡) IDs are often shared instead of — or alongside — phone numbers.
c.ctaFinalSub: Ready for more? Try the medium exercises covering bigger numbers and phone numbers.
c.nativeIntro: Native Korean numbers are used for counting things, age, and hours. They're irregular and a bit harder, but you only need to know 1 to 10 to cover most daily situations. Here are the first five:
c.tipWhenToUse: Rule of thumb: if you're counting OBJECTS or talking about AGE / HOURS, use native numbers (하나, 둘, 셋…). For everything else — money, dates, minutes, phone numbers, math — use Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼…).

hiragana.title: Hiragana
hiragana.desc: Master the 46 phonetic kana — the first script every Japanese learner needs.

section.introP1: Hiragana is the cursive Japanese phonetic script, born in the Heian period (794–1185). Each kana evolved as a stylised, flowing version of a Chinese character used purely for its sound — for instance あ comes from 安, か from 加, さ from 左. Over a couple of centuries the brush-written shapes drifted further and further from their kanji origins until they became their own independent system of 46 sounds.
section.introP2: Hiragana was originally called onnade ("women's hand") because Heian-period women — barred from the formal Chinese-language education reserved for men — used it to write poetry, diaries and the world's first novels. Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji and Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book were written almost entirely in hiragana, and they're considered foundational works of world literature.
section.introP3: Today hiragana is the first script every Japanese child learns. It's used to write native Japanese words that have no kanji form, grammatical particles and inflections, furigana reading hints above kanji, and any text aimed at young readers or learners. If you can read hiragana, you can read aloud anything written in Japanese — even if you don't know the kanji.

katakana.title: Katakana
katakana.desc: The 46 angular kana used for loanwords, names and emphasis.

section.introP1: Katakana was developed in the Heian period by Buddhist monks who needed a fast, compact way to annotate Chinese sutras with Japanese pronunciation guides. Rather than reusing the cursive women's hiragana, they took a single radical out of each Chinese character and used it as a phonetic shorthand — for example イ is the left half of 伊, ロ comes from 呂, ヌ is the bottom of 奴.
section.introP2: The name katakana literally means "fragmentary kana" (片 kata = piece, 仮名 kana = borrowed name), reflecting the script's origin as kanji fragments. The angular, geometric strokes are a direct legacy of those rapid brush annotations — every katakana can be drawn in just a few decisive lines, in stark contrast to the flowing hiragana.
section.introP3: In modern Japanese, katakana is reserved for: foreign loanwords (コーヒー "coffee", テレビ "television"), foreign personal and place names, the names of plants and animals in scientific contexts, onomatopoeia (ワンワン "woof woof"), and emphasis — the same role italics play in English. Knowing katakana is essential for navigating menus, packaging and tech vocabulary in Japan.

level1.title: Level 1 (JLPT N5)
level1.desc: Master the foundations — introducing yourself, daily expressions, and the most essential vocabulary.

intro.description: Start your Japanese journey with the essentials. By the end of this level, you'll know how to greet, introduce yourself, and handle basic everyday interactions with confidence.
intro.obj1: Greet people at any time of day
intro.obj2: Say thank you, sorry, and excuse me
intro.obj3: Introduce yourself and ask basic questions
intro.obj4: Express yes, no, and polite requests
intro.officialInfo: JLPT N5 is the entry level of the Japan Foundation's official Japanese proficiency test, recognized worldwide. It certifies your ability to understand basic Japanese — daily greetings, simple conversations, and reading hiragana, katakana, and ~100 basic kanji. N5 is often required for the Specified Skilled Worker visa (SSW), N4-N2 for most work and study visas, and N1 awards points under the Highly Skilled Professional visa system.

c.intro: In this first lesson you'll learn the essential greetings and how to introduce yourself in Japanese. We'll use the polite forms most appropriate for daily life, work, and meeting new people.
c.greetExplain: Unlike English's single "hello", Japanese uses three different greetings depending on the time of day. おはようございます is the most formal, used at the office or with strangers. In informal settings (friends, family), you can shorten it to just おはよう.
c.tipOhayou: おはようございます literally means "it's early". You'll hear workers say it even in the afternoon when arriving at a shift — it works as a "hi, I'm here!" in work contexts.
c.prGreetQ1: At 8 AM, you meet your colleague.
c.prGreetQ2: At 2 PM, you enter a shop.
c.selfExplain: This is the most fundamental Japanese sentence structure. わたし (watashi) means "I", は (wa) is the topic marker (written with the hiragana は but pronounced "wa"), and です (desu) is the copula meaning "is/am". Replace [name] with your name, your job, your nationality, etc.
c.prSelfQ1: わたしは ___ です。(your name)
c.prSelfQ2: わたしは ___ です。(your job)
c.ctaMidSub: Lock in greetings and the XはYです pattern with some easy exercises.
c.lblPleased: nice to meet you (literal: please treat me well)
c.meetExplain: When meeting someone for the first time, Japanese people follow a specific ritual: say はじめまして (nice to meet you / this is the first time), introduce yourself, then close with どうぞよろしく おねがいします (please treat me well — a polite formula that has no direct English equivalent).
c.dlgMeet2: Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka.
c.dlgMeet4: Please treat me well. (pleased to meet you)
c.cultureBowText: A slight bow (15°) is customary when meeting someone new, thanking, or apologizing. In business, the depth and duration of the bow indicate the level of respect. Don't worry about getting it perfect as a beginner — a sincere small bow is always appreciated. Handshakes are becoming more common in international contexts.
c.thankExplain: ありがとうございます is the formal way to say thank you. The informal version ありがとう is fine among friends. すみません is incredibly versatile — it means sorry, excuse me, and can even be used as "thank you" when someone goes out of their way for you (acknowledging the inconvenience you caused).
c.tipSumimasen: すみません is one of the most useful Japanese words ever. Use it to: (1) get someone's attention (like "excuse me, waiter"), (2) apologize for bumping into someone, (3) thank someone for going out of their way, (4) squeeze past someone in a crowd. When in doubt, say すみません!
c.exRepeat: Sorry, could you say that again please?
c.byeExplain: さようなら is the textbook "goodbye" but it carries a sense of finality — Japanese people actually rarely use it in daily life except when you won't see someone for a long time. In most casual contexts, Japanese people use softer farewells depending on when they'll see each other again.
c.byeOyasumi: Good night (when parting in the evening)
c.cultureByeText: Japanese people often accompany goodbyes with a slight bow. In professional contexts, the lower-ranking person waits for the higher-ranking one to leave first. When leaving work, you'll hear おつかれさまでした (you must be tired — thanks for your hard work) — a specific phrase for leaving the workplace that doesn't translate directly.
c.ctaFinalSub: Challenge yourself with medium-level exercises covering everything from this lesson.

c.intro: In this lesson you'll learn how to talk about the objects around you: "this", "that near you", "that over there". You'll also learn how to ask "what is this?" and how to show ownership with the particle の.
c.demoExplain: Japanese has three distance-based demonstratives: これ (kore) for things near the speaker, それ (sore) for things near the listener, and あれ (are) for things far from both. They replace entire nouns, unlike English "this/that" which stands alongside a noun.
c.tipKoSoA: The ko-so-a pattern runs through many Japanese words: これ/それ/あれ (this/that/that over there), ここ/そこ/あそこ (here/there/over there), この/その/あの + noun (this/that/that ... noun). Learn them together — the logic transfers directly.
c.prDemoQ1: You point at a pen next to your friend. How do you say "that is a pen"?
c.prDemoQ2: Type the word for "that (near the listener)".
c.qExplain: なん/なに (nan/nani) means "what". Before です it's pronounced なん. Add か at the end of a sentence to turn it into a question — no intonation change or question mark needed.
c.dlg3: Is that over there a business card too?
c.dlg4: No, that one is a card.
c.ctaMidSub: Lock in demonstratives and questions before we tackle possessives.
c.boardNoTitle: A の B — "B belonging to / of A"
c.noExplain: The particle の links two nouns: the first describes or owns the second. わたしの かばん (my bag), 日本の くるま (Japanese car), 日本語の じしょ (Japanese dictionary). It's the single most useful particle in the language — start overusing it.
c.tipNo: If the thing being described is already clear from context, you can drop it: これは わたしの です = "this is mine". The の acts as a pronoun.
c.prNoQ1: わたし___ かばんです。 (type the particle)
c.prNoA2: わたしの ほんです。
c.cultureTitle: On giving things & the の particle
c.cultureText: Japanese people often use の to soften questions about ownership: これは だれの ですか (whose is this?) feels less direct than asking the owner's name outright. When offering or pointing at things, it's polite to identify the owner rather than the object itself.
c.ctaFinalSub: Mixed exercises on demonstratives, questions, and の.

c.intro: This lesson teaches how to point out places (here/there/over there), ask where something is, ask prices, and describe things by origin or type.
c.placeExplain: ここ, そこ, あそこ work exactly like これ/それ/あれ but refer to places instead of things. Ask "where?" with どこ.
c.tipDoko: どこ = where. どれ = which one (of many). Don't confuse them.
c.prPlaceQ1: You're asking where the bank is.
c.prPlaceA1: ぎんこうは どこですか。
c.prPlaceOpt2: ぎんこうは だれですか。
c.prPlaceOpt3: ぎんこうは なんですか。
c.prPlaceOpt4: ぎんこうは どうですか。
c.priceExplain: いくら means "how much". Japanese prices are in yen (えん, 円). Numbers are read in multiples of 万 (10,000) — e.g. 30,000 = 3万 (san-man).
c.dlg1: Excuse me, how much is this?
c.tipKudasai: 〜を ください literally means "please give me ~". Use it to ask for anything in shops, restaurants, or when making polite requests.
c.countryExplain: Use [A]の[B] to describe origin (日本の くるま — a Japanese car), type (コーヒーの カップ — a coffee cup), or any descriptive noun relationship.
c.cultureText: Japanese floor numbers follow the American convention: 1st floor (1かい) is ground level. Many office buildings have no 4th floor (4 sounds like "death", し), jumping straight to 5.
c.ctaFinalSub: Places + prices + origins in one go.

ex.e5q: How do you ask for something politely in a shop?
ex.e5b: これは どこですか。
ex.e5d: これは いくらですか。

ex.m5a: これは いくらですか。
ex.m5b: これは どこですか。
ex.m5d: これは だれですか。
ex.h4src: The meeting room is on the 2nd floor.

c.intro: Telling time, talking about daily activities, and introducing the polite ます-form with its four tenses: present, negative, past, past negative.
c.timeExplain: Hours use じ (-ji). 4時 is read よじ (yo-ji), 7時 is しちじ, 9時 is くじ. Half past is はん (han). Use ごぜん/ごご for AM/PM.
c.tipReadings: Irregular time readings: 4時 = よじ, 7時 = しちじ, 9時 = くじ. Minutes ending in 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 often pronounced ぷん; 2, 5, 7, 9 → ふん. Listen carefully.
c.boardVerbTitle: Four tenses of the polite verb
c.verbExplain: Every polite verb ends in ます. Swap the endings for negative / past / past negative: ます → ません → ました → ませんでした. Use に after a specific time.
c.tipNi: Use に with specific times (6時に), days (月曜日に), birthdays (たんじょうびに). Don't use に with vague time words like きょう, あした, いま.
c.exMorning: I wake up at 6 every morning.
c.prVerbQ2: What's the past-tense polite form of たべます?
c.dlg1: Mr. Miller, what hours do you work every day?
c.dlg3: Are Saturdays and Sundays your days off?
c.cultureText: Traditional Japanese office hours run 9 to 18, but lingering after hours ("ざんぎょう") is still common. The phrase おつかれさまでした ("thanks for your hard work") is used when leaving — you'll hear it daily.
c.ctaFinalSub: Time, verbs, days — mixed medium exercises.

c.intro: Learn to talk about destinations with へ, transportation with で, companions with と, and ask when / where / with whom.
c.goExplain: Use へ (pronounced "e") after a place to mark direction. Three key verbs: いきます (go), きます (come), かえります (go home / return).
c.tipHe: へ is written with the hiragana he but pronounced "e" — like the topic marker は is written ha but pronounced "wa". Particles have phonetic quirks.
c.exGoDept: Today I'm going to the department store.
c.meansExplain: で after a transport noun marks how you travel. Exception: "on foot" uses あるいて (not あしで).
c.tipAruite: あるいて is the て-form of あるきます (to walk). You'll learn the full て-form rule later — for now memorize it as "on foot".
c.exByTrain: I go to the office by train.
c.exByTaxi: I went to the hotel by taxi.
c.prA3: バスで うちへ かえります。
c.prOpt2: バスに うちへ かえります。
c.prOpt3: バスへ うちで かえります。
c.prOpt4: バスへ うちに かえります。
c.ctaMidSub: へ, で — destinations and means.
c.withExplain: と marks "together with". ひとりで means "alone". いつ means "when?".
c.dlg1: Mr. Miller, where are you going tomorrow?
c.cultureText: Shinkansen tickets are precise: assigned seat, car number, departure minute. Trains leave to the second — if you're not on the platform 30 seconds early, you'll watch it pull away. Station staff bow to each departing train.

ex.e2q: Which particle marks means of transport?
ex.m2src: I'm going to Kyoto with a friend.
ex.m5q: What does ひとりで mean?
ex.h1src: I went with my family by shinkansen.
ex.h4src: I went to the hotel by taxi.
ex.h5q: How is the particle へ pronounced?

c.intro: Learn the direct-object particle を, the place-of-action で, and how to invite someone with ませんか / ましょう.
c.objExplain: を marks the direct object of a transitive verb: what you eat, drink, buy, read, write, see. Written with hiragana を but pronounced "o".
c.tipWo: Only を — never お — is used as a particle, even though both sound the same. Getting this right when writing is a core beginner rule.
c.whereExplain: で marks the place where an action happens — distinct from へ (destination) and に (existence location).
c.exLunchResto: I eat lunch at a restaurant.
c.exReadLib: I read books at the library.
c.exBuyVeg: I buy vegetables at the supermarket.
c.ctaMidSub: を, で — objects and action places.
c.inviteExplain: ませんか is a polite invitation ("won't you…?"). ましょう means "let's". Use ましょうか to suggest with slight doubt ("shall we?").
c.tipInvite: Responses: いいですね (sounds good!) to accept, すみません、ちょっと… to decline politely (literally "sorry, a bit…").
c.dlg1: Mr. Miller, won't you eat lunch with me?
c.dlg2: Sounds good. What shall we eat?
c.cultureText: Japanese rarely say "no" directly. すみません、ちょっと… trailing off is a clear refusal. The key is to signal the discomfort — the other person understands and gracefully backs off without forcing a reason.

ex.e1q: Which particle marks a direct object?
ex.e2q: Where does the action happen with で?
ex.h1src: I ate dinner at a restaurant.
ex.h4src: I watched a movie with my friend.
ex.h5q: Written form of the object particle (o)?

c.intro: Using the で particle for tools, に for recipients, and verbs of giving (あげます) and receiving (もらいます). Plus もう / まだ (already / not yet).
c.toolExplain: で also marks the instrument or tool of an action: "with chopsticks", "with a computer", "in English".
c.exPc: I write letters with the computer.
c.prToolA2: 日本語で かきます。
c.prToolOpt2: 日本語に かきます。
c.prToolOpt3: 日本語を かきます。
c.prToolOpt4: 日本語は かきます。
c.giveExplain: あげます (give) takes the recipient with に. もらいます (receive) takes the giver with に or から (から is preferred for distant / formal sources).
c.tipGive: Never use あげます for gifts given to you — use もらいます instead. Japanese strictly tracks the direction of giving; getting it wrong sounds rude.
c.exGaveFlower: I gave my friend a flower.
c.exGotPresent: I received a present from Mr. Tanaka.
c.exLearnJp: I learn Japanese from my teacher.
c.alreadyExplain: もう + [past polite verb] = "already ~". まだです = "not yet". Handy for scheduling and checking in.
c.dlg1: Mr. Miller, have you already eaten lunch?
c.cultureText: Omiyage (souvenirs from trips) are nearly mandatory among Japanese colleagues. Always brought back individually wrapped so everyone in the office gets a bite. Refusing a gift takes great tact — it's almost always accepted.

ex.e2q: Which particle marks the receiver of a gift?
ex.e5q: What does ならいます mean?
ex.m2src: I gave my friend a book.
ex.m3q: You received a present from Tanaka. Which verb?
ex.m5q: What does もう mean in "もう たべました"?
ex.h1src: I learn Japanese from my teacher.
ex.h4src: I wrote a letter on the computer.

c.intro: Japanese has two adjective families: い-adjectives and な-adjectives. Each conjugates differently. Learn both, plus how to describe experiences with どう / とても / あまり.
c.iExplain: い-adjectives always end in い in dictionary form. To make them negative, replace い with くない: たかい → たかくない. Add です for politeness.
c.tipII: The word いい (good) is irregular. Its negative is よくない, its past is よかった (never いかった). Memorize the exceptions.
c.naExplain: な-adjectives act like nouns. Add です for the sentence end. Add な when attaching directly to a noun: しずかな まち (a quiet town). Negative: じゃありません or じゃないです.
c.tipKirei: Watch out: きれい ends in い but is a な-adjective. ゆうめい, きらい, and a few others trap beginners. Memorize the tricky ones.
c.prOpt2: おいしいじゃないです
c.prOpt4: おいしいじゃありません
c.prQ3: Negate あつい politely: あつ___です
c.howExplain: どうですか = "how is it?". とても = very. あまり + negative = not very. けど links two adjectives ("A but B").
c.dlg1: Mr. Miller, how's life in Japan?
c.cultureTitle: The すてき vs きれい nuance
c.cultureText: Both praise things favorably, but きれい leans toward visual beauty and cleanliness, while すてき is broader — wonderful, tasteful, classy. Use すてき for a friend's new outfit; use きれい for a garden.

ex.e1q: Which ends in い but is a な-adjective?
ex.e5q: Which is the negative of しずか?
ex.e5c: しずかじゃ ありません
ex.m3q: Connect a な-adjective to a noun — which is correct?
ex.h4src: Mr. Miller is handsome and kind.

c.intro: Express what you like, what you're good at, what you understand, and give reasons with から.
c.sukiExplain: Some "feelings" adjectives take が instead of を for their object: すき (like), きらい (dislike), じょうず (good at), へた (bad at). They're all な-adjectives.
c.tipGa: Why が instead of を? These are feelings / abilities — not actions. Japanese treats the thing liked as the subject of the emotion, not the object of an action.
c.exDance: Mr. Miller is good at dancing.
c.prSukiA2: わたしは スポーツが へたです。
c.prSukiOpt2: わたしは スポーツを へたです。
c.prSukiOpt3: わたしは スポーツに へたです。
c.prSukiOpt4: わたしが スポーツは へたです。
c.boardHaveTitle: わかります / あります
c.haveExplain: わかります (understand) and あります (have / exist) also take が for their object. Use に with the subject if needed: わたしに おかねが ありません.
c.whyExplain: End a sentence with から to give a reason: "because ~". Use どうして to ask why.
c.tipKara: から goes at the end of the reason clause, not the main clause: "I can't come because I'm busy" = いそがしいから 行けません. Don't translate literally from English.
c.dlg1: Mr. Miller, won't you come to karaoke tonight?
c.dlg4: Because I have a lot of work.
c.cultureText: Japanese karaoke happens in private rooms (カラオケボックス), not on a public stage. Everyone takes turns — skipping yours is rude. Applause after each song is expected. The "perfect score" (100点) is a shared celebration moment.

ex.e2q: What does じょうず mean?
ex.m2src: Mr. Miller is good at Japanese.
ex.m3q: Which particle with わかります?
ex.m5q: から appears at which position?
ex.h1src: Because I have a lot of work.
ex.h5q: How to say "I don't like tomatoes"?
ex.h5a: トマトを きらいです。
ex.h5b: トマトが きらいです。
ex.h5c: トマトは きらいに です。
ex.h5d: トマトで きらいです。

c.intro: Japanese distinguishes "existing" for animate (います) and inanimate (あります). Plus position words (above, below, next to, between…) for describing locations.
c.shExistsTitle: います vs あります
c.existsExplain: Use います for people, animals, anything that moves on its own. Use あります for objects, plants (they don't move), abstract things like appointments, money, time.
c.tipPlant: Tricky case: plants use あります (they don't walk around). Robots and stuffed toys use あります too — but your pet cat takes います.
c.exDogPark: There's a dog in the park.
c.exEggFridge: There are eggs in the fridge.
c.exMikeRoom: Mr. Miller is in the room.
c.prExistsA1: ぞう が います
c.prExistsOpt2: ぞう が あります
c.prExistsOpt3: ぞう を います
c.prExistsOpt4: ぞう の います
c.prExistsQ2: Type the correct verb: ねこが ___ (at the door)
c.whereExplain: Position is expressed as "X の [ue/shita/mae/ushiro/migi/hidari/naka/soto/tonari/chikaku/aida] に". The position word is a noun — connect it with の.
c.exCatTable: The cat is under the table.
c.exMailbox: The mailbox is in front of the building.
c.exBetween: The coffee shop is between the bookstore and the building.
c.askExplain: [thing] は どこに ありますか is the standard "where is ~?" question. Follow up with ちかくに (nearby?) or となりに (next to?) to localize further.
c.dlg1: Excuse me, where is the post office?
c.dlg2: It's in front of the station.
c.dlg4: Yes, it's next to the post office.
c.cultureText: Japanese addresses use district / block / building numbers — not street names. Locals often give directions by landmark ("next to the コンビニ across from the station") rather than streets. Don't expect a street name.

ex.e1q: Which verb for a living being?
ex.e2q: Which verb for a book on a shelf?
ex.m2src: The mailbox is in front of the building.
ex.m3q: Which particle marks where something exists?
ex.h1src: The coffee shop is between the bookstore and the building.
ex.h4src: There's no one in the room.
ex.h5b: えきの まえに あります
